idiom_name: none - the JVM guarantees one heap object per instance; the substitutes are primitive-specialized storage and caching
alternative: Primitive specialization and arrays instead of small boxed values (int[]/long[] or a specialized collection library), the JIT's escape analysis for genuinely non-escaping values, and pooling or off-heap storage (ByteBuffer, MemorySegment) where identity must go away; Project Valhalla value classes (JEP 401, preview) are the eventual language-level answer, and until they ship a hand-rolled inline buffer cannot be expressed.
implementation_notes: On the JVM every object has identity and lives on the heap, so a type cannot embed a variable-size payload: there is no union, no inline array inside an object, and no value type before Valhalla - JEP 401 is still a preview feature and explicitly does not guarantee any particular layout, though its motivation is precisely the pointer-chasing and allocation cost of small immutable values such as LocalDate. The JIT's escape analysis can scalar-replace allocations that do not escape, but that is a runtime optimization, not a representation the program can choose or rely on. What the platform really offers for small values is sharing and specialization: Integer.valueOf 'will always cache values in the range -128 to 127', String is compact (a byte[] plus a coder) but still a heap object, and primitive-collection libraries or off-heap buffers keep small records dense. Treat the classic structure as unavailable and pick one of those substitutes instead.
pitfalls: The Integer cache is a fixed-size identity trick, not an inline buffer: relying on == for boxed values works only inside -128..127, and the same trap reappears with any value-based class whose factory caches - use equals(), never identity, as a correctness rule.

Escape analysis is a JIT decision: the same method can allocate in the interpreter and scalar-replace later, so 'it does not allocate' is true only for a given JIT and version - never build an API contract or a benchmark conclusion on it.

Boxing hides allocations everywhere (generics, lambda captures, varargs, records with boxed fields): a designed-for-density representation is lost the moment a value is passed as Object, so keep small values in primitive arrays end to end.
sources: OpenJDK, JEP 401: Value Objects (Preview) - objects that lack identity can be represented by the JVM in ways that improve memory footprint and locality, and it is 'not a goal to guarantee any particular optimization strategy or memory layout': https://openjdk.org/jeps/401

Oracle Java SE API, Integer.valueOf(int) - 'This method will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive, and may cache other values outside of this range': https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Integer.html#valueOf(int)
